01 ★ Flagship · UVM + Formal

AHB-to-APB Bridge: Design, UVM Verification & Formal Sign-off

RTL design, UVM coverage closure, and formal property proof

The AHB-to-APB bridge sits at the boundary of ARM's AMBA fabric, translating pipelined high-speed AHB transactions into the two-phase (SETUP, ENABLE) APB protocol through an 8-state control FSM. I owned this design end to end: RTL implementation, a layered UVM verification environment, and formal sign-off across two industry tools.

Verification Plan & Methodology
  • Wrote a feature-extracted verification plan mapping every protocol behavior (address phase, data phase, wait-state insertion, error response) to a checker and a coverage point, so closure was measured against intent rather than raw stimulus.
  • Architected a layered UVM environment with independent AHB and APB agents (driver, monitor, sequencer), a virtual sequencer for cross-interface coordination, a predictor-based scoreboard, and a reference model for transaction-level checking.
  • Drove constrained-random traffic with layered sequences and directed corner cases (back-to-back transfers, stalled PREADY, reset mid-transaction), closing functional and code coverage with covergroups and cross coverage on transfer type, response, and wait-state depth.
  • Proved the environment's detection strength through deliberate bug injection, confirming the scoreboard and assertions flagged each seeded fault.
Formal Property Verification
  • Wrote intent-driven SVA covering FSM transition safety, mutually-exclusive one-hot PSEL decode, handshake liveness, and data-integrity invariants across the bridge, bound to the DUT so the RTL stayed untouched.
  • Tuned input assumptions to the minimal constraint set that avoids over-constraining while still ruling out illegal stimulus, the key to clean proof convergence in both tools.
  • Ran in Synopsys VC Formal and Cadence JasperGold; root-caused a class of failing assertions to an overlapping vs. non-overlapping implication mismatch against the design's combinational sensitivity, then reached full proof with no remaining counterexamples.
  • Added AEP FSM deadlock analysis (every critical state proven exit-safe) and a JasperGold X-propagation run confirming deterministic outputs and FSM state after reset.

02

AXI4 Crossbar: Formal Property Verification

White-box SVA proof of a parametric NxM interconnect

Bottom-up formal sign-off of a parametric AXI4 / AXI4-Lite crossbar, done entirely in JasperGold with no simulation testbenches. Properties bind to the DUT through SVA bind files, mirroring how verification runs when RTL ownership sits with a separate team. Five property suites were written across the interconnect — the shared FIFO, the master write and read switches, the round-robin arbiter, and the slave-side out-of-order completion tracker — each checking real, observable input/output behavior (a specific request pattern producing a specific grant) rather than just comparing internal wires to one another.

Verified Scope
  • Shared FIFO (axicb_scfifo) — the buffering primitive reused across every AW/W/B/AR/R channel, the write switch's grant FIFO, and the slave path's per-ID FIFO.
  • Master write switch (axicb_mst_switch_wr) — AW arbitration, W-channel ordering, and ID-mask B-response routing.
  • Master read switch (axicb_mst_switch_rd) — AR arbitration and ID-mask R-response routing.
  • Priority round-robin arbiter (axicb_round_robin) — one-hot grant, mask rotation, four priority layers, and bounded liveness.
  • Slave out-of-order completion tracker (axicb_slv_ooo) — per-ID outstanding tracking, completion routing, and misrouted-transaction priority.
Verification Strategy
  • Wrote every suite as a partitioned set of assumptions, assertions, and cover properties, favoring properties that check observable I/O behavior over ones that merely restate the RTL's own if/else logic as an assertion — more work to write, but what actually gives confidence the design does what it should.
  • Verified the shared FIFO (axicb_scfifo) fully standalone — push, pull, data, and flush all left free with no borrowed assumptions — so a real bug cannot hide behind a convenient constraint. This is the FIFO reused everywhere: AW/W/B/AR/R buffering, the grant FIFO in the write switch, and the per-ID FIFO in the out-of-order slave path.
  • Applied a two-pass abstraction strategy on the write-path switch to keep both proofs converging: Pass 1 black-boxes the write-data FIFO (reset tied off, full-flag forced low) to prove AW arbitration and B-routing on their own; Pass 2 opens the FIFO to prove W-channel ordering and FIFO integrity.
  • Bound the priority round-robin arbiter with full white-box visibility into the mask/grant internals across all four priority layers — fairness is effectively impossible to check as a black box, since you need the mask register to know whether the grant is actually rotating.
FIFO — axicb_scfifo
  • Reset behavior checked as three separate properties (async reset, sync reset, flush), since each path clears the pointers a slightly different way in the RTL — not assumed equivalent just because they look similar.
  • Overflow / underflow protection is the property set that matters most: pushing into a full FIFO must not move the write pointer and pulling from an empty FIFO must not move the read pointer — if either ever fires, that is silent data corruption, exactly the bug you don't want to find in silicon.
  • Data integrity proven with a shadow memory built only from ports and bound-in pointers (never touching the DUT's real RAM), checking that data_out always matches what was written to a slot and never drifts on its own before the front entry is popped.
  • Flag and pointer correctness: empty/full checked against the actual pointer math, full and empty never both true, and the extra-bit trick that distinguishes full from empty verified to flip at exactly the right moment and nowhere else. Cover properties confirm the FIFO can fill completely, drain back to empty, and wrap both pointers at least once.
Master Write Switch — axicb_mst_switch_wr
  • Grant / AW correctness: the grant vector is always one-hot or all-zero, whatever it points to is what appears on the output AW fields (no crosstalk), and awready never returns to a master that wasn't granted — otherwise two masters could both believe they won arbitration.
  • W follows AW: once a master wins AW and the handshake completes, W data must come from that same master. Pass 2 adds FIFO-gated checks — the grant FIFO that remembers who won is never pushed when full nor pulled when empty, and its output payload/wlast really belongs to whoever is at the front.
  • B-channel routing via the ID-mask scheme: bvalid only ever reaches the one master whose ID mask matches, bready is forwarded from the actual target, and the B payload passes through unmangled.
  • Cover set confirms every master gets at least one AW handshake, back-to-back handshakes occur, all masters can request at once (the real stress case), and — in Pass 2 — a full AW → W → B transaction completes end to end with the write FIFO reaching full.
Round-Robin Arbiter — axicb_round_robin
  • One-hot mutual exclusion — never grant two requesters at once, never grant someone not requesting — plus mask correctness: after a grant the mask shifts that requester to the back of the line, reboots to zero once it walks past the MSB, and always keeps its expected all-ones-then-all-zeros shape rather than a garbled pattern.
  • Fairness and rotation: the masked path (skip anyone already served this round) is taken before the unmasked wraparound fallback, and the same requester is not granted twice in a row unless it is genuinely the only one asking — this is where it earns the name "round robin" rather than being priority arbitration with extra steps.
  • Priority layers (P0 lowest → P3 highest) verified so higher always beats lower and the grant genuinely comes from the active layer's own grant vector, not leaked from elsewhere.
  • Bounded liveness / no starvation: requesting at the highest active priority guarantees a grant within REQ_NB cycles, and same-priority peers don't starve past 2×REQ_NB cycles — the fairness half of the proof, checked as a real bound since formal tools need one.
Master Read Switch & Slave OOO Tracker
  • The read switch (axicb_mst_switch_rd) mirrors the AW/B checks for AR/R but is structurally simpler — R responses already carry the requesting master's ID, so no grant-memory FIFO is needed and it proves in a single pass over the full state space. rlast gets the same treatment as rvalid: gated by both ID-match and o_rvalid.
  • The out-of-order completion tracker (axicb_slv_ooo) is the harder slave-side counterpart: it tracks one outstanding transaction per ID in a per-ID FIFO and arbitrates round-robin which ID's completion returns next. Its core anti-crosstalk property checks a completion request never fires unless a slave is actually valid, actually the targeted one, and actually carrying that slot's own unmasked ID — checked against an independently re-derived reference, not a copy of the RTL's own computation. Misrouted transactions (targeting no real slave) are served ahead of everything else, verified as a genuine priority property.
Counterexamples Found & Fixed
  • The first full run of the read-switch suite returned 7 CEX out of 131 checks, each traced back to the RTL rather than weakened until it passed. One property (ast_arvalid_out_clears_after_srst) turned out not to be a real invariant and was deleted; two others were genuine invariants that only broke when sync-reset fired mid-transaction, so reset was added to disable iff on exactly those two rather than blanket-disabling the file.
  • The remaining four (ast_rlast_requires_rvalid, one per master) exposed a genuine RTL bug: i_rlast[i] was computed from ID-mask targeting alone, without also gating on o_rvalid the way i_rvalid[i] already was — so it could glitch high while rvalid stayed low. Harmless in practice, but a real asymmetry, so it was fixed at the RTL. A follow-up re-run then surfaced a fifth property written against the old behavior, which was updated to match the now-correct RTL. Final run: 129 checks, 53 proven, 75 covered, 0 CEX.
  • The slave-OOO suite surfaced a related class of mistake: an "obvious" wiring-sanity property (ast_idgrant_zero_when_no_creqs) that assumed grant tracks request combinationally every cycle — but the arbiter core's grant output holds its last latched value while its enable is low, fully decoupled from request. The fix adds the missing c_en qualifier to the antecedent, the same enable idiom every request/grant property in the arbiter suite already uses.

03

EvoAI: Hardware-Accelerated Genetic Algorithm

HW/SW co-design · Cocotb verification · OpenLane synthesis

A hardware/software co-design that accelerates the most compute-intensive stage of a genetic algorithm, mutation, by offloading it to a synthesizable FSM while Python orchestrates selection, crossover, and fitness evaluation. My entry point into hardware for AI workloads.

Design & Verification Approach
  • Profiled the pure-Python GA with cProfile / tracemalloc and identified mutation as the dominant runtime bottleneck, the data-driven justification for moving it to hardware.
  • Implemented the mutation block as a character-wise SystemVerilog FSM driven by LFSR pseudo-randomness, with flattened gene buses and a valid/done handshake.
  • Built a self-checking Cocotb testbench that bridges the Python golden model and the DUT, comparing hardware output against the reference per gene and validating the handshake protocol end to end.
  • Pushed the verified RTL through full ASIC implementation with OpenLane on Sky130, taking the block from behavioral model to synthesized layout.

04

Last-Level Cache: MESI Coherence Model

16 MB, 16-way set-associative LLC in SystemVerilog

A cycle-behavioral model of a last-level cache that sits between an L1 and a shared system bus, maintaining coherence with the MESI protocol while servicing processor requests and bus-side snoops.

Design & Verification Approach
  • Designed a 16 MB, 16-way set-associative cache with 64-byte lines, write-allocate / write-back policy, and pseudo-LRU replacement across 16,384 sets.
  • Implemented all 9 request types (reads, writes, snooped read / write / RWIM, invalidate) with full MESI state transitions and bus-operation reporting.
  • Wrote a trace-driven verification suite targeting every coherence state transition, including snoop-induced downgrades and false-sharing cases, with self-checking against expected MESI state and hit/miss outcome.
  • Validated cache statistics (hit rate, eviction counts) against a golden reference and root-caused coherence mismatches down to the offending transition, the debug discipline that matters most in coherence verification.

05

Post-Silicon Validation Tool: IA-32 Generator

Runtime machine-code generation & execution in C

A C framework that models post-silicon validation by dynamically generating real IA-32 machine code at runtime, executing it from mmap'd executable memory, and checking instruction-level behavior, the kind of low-level bring-up testing used when first silicon arrives.

Validation Approach
  • Wrote an IA-32 / x86-64 encoding library that assembles binary opcodes directly (MOV forms, atomics like XADD / XCHG, and memory fences MFENCE / SFENCE / LFENCE) using ModR/M, REX prefixes, and operand-size overrides.
  • Generated randomized instruction streams from a seeded RNG for reproducible, systematic instruction-level coverage and repeatable failure replay.
  • Exercised single- and multi-threaded modes through fork + pthread barriers with per-thread CPU affinity to stress concurrency and memory-ordering behavior across cores.
  • Verified the encoded streams in GDB by disassembling the live buffer and confirming each instruction matched its intended encoding, the validation-vs-golden discipline at the heart of silicon bring-up.

06

Gshare–Perceptron Hybrid Branch Predictor

Five predictors benchmarked across six workload traces

A microarchitecture study implementing and comparing five branch predictors, culminating in a custom hybrid that combines Gshare's global-history correlation with a perceptron's ability to learn linearly-separable patterns. Written up as an academic submission.

Approach
  • Implemented 2-bit bimodal, Gshare, perceptron, tournament, and a custom hybrid predictor in a common simulation framework with a consistent storage-cost model for fair comparison.
  • The hybrid uses a chooser table of saturating counters to arbitrate between Gshare and the perceptron per branch, capturing both short-range correlation and long linear history.
  • Evaluated across six traces (FP, integer, multimedia), measuring accuracy, total mispredictions, and MPKI; the hybrid delivered the most consistent accuracy and rode through misprediction spikes most smoothly.

07

RV32I RISC-V ISA Simulator

Modular fetch–decode–execute simulator in C

A functional instruction-set simulator for the RV32I base integer subset of RISC-V, built as a clean fetch → decode → execute loop with independently testable subsystems.

Approach
  • Modeled a 32-entry register file, byte-addressable memory, and program counter, supporting all six instruction formats (R, I, S, B, U, J) loaded from .mem images.
  • Split the design into independently unit-tested modules (decode, execute, memory) with dedicated test executables for parsing, memory, loads, and stores.
  • Added verbose, debug, and single-step modes for per-instruction register tracing, enabling ISA-compliance checking and root-cause analysis of incorrect behavior.
